# Electrical Problems After Auto Start Installation

Intermittent power loss on a 2000 Camry following an RS90 remote starter installation points to a specific wiring topology rather than a random electrical failure. The symptomsâdead dash, inoperative windows and turn signals, yet functioning headlights, brake lights, dome light, and stereoâare classic indicators of a compromised ignition-switched power rail. These components rely entirely on the "ACC" or accessory circuit for voltage, whereas headlamps and tail lamps often draw from the battery directly via a constant fuse or a separate ignition feed.

When the vehicle refused to shift out of Park and required manual intervention via the shift lock release button, the issue was likely compounded by a safety interlock that detects an active immobilizer state or insufficient voltage to disengage the locking solenoid. The fact that the car started after being parked overnight suggests a thermal drift issue: components expand when hot and contract when cool, potentially creating momentary open circuits in tight harnesses or failing connections at splice points.

The root cause almost certainly lies in how the RS90 was integrated into the existing wiring harness. Most universal remote starter kits operate by tapping into the ignition switch wires to detect "ON" status for engine start and "ACC" status for accessory power. If the installer connected the remote starter's blue wire (commonly used for ACC detection) incorrectly, or if they spliced directly into a single fused line that supplies multiple critical modules without adequate gauge capacity, they could have introduced a high-resistance joint.

A high-resistance connection acts like a voltage divider. When the ignition is turned to "ACC" or "ON," the current draw from the dash cluster, ECU, and window motors spikes. If the splice point has poor contactâperhaps due to stripped insulation, oxidation, or insufficient crimpingâthe voltage drop across that specific joint can exceed the threshold required for sensitive electronics to operate, effectively cutting power to those circuits while leaving heavy-draw loads like headlights unaffected.

The intermittent nature of the failure reinforces this diagnosis. Heat generated by current flow through a bad splice increases resistance further as the car sits, or conversely, thermal expansion separates a loose connection when the engine is hot. Once the vehicle cools overnight, the metal contracts, restoring contact temporarily. This is why the system functioned normally after an overnight park but failed later that day.

To resolve this without uninstalling the unit, you must inspect every splice made during the installation of the RS90. Focus specifically on connections where the harness was opened to tap into factory wires. Use a multimeter to check for continuity and measure voltage drop across each connection while the ignition is on. You are looking for joints that show significant resistance or voltage loss under load. If a splice is found, redo it using proper heat-shrink butt connectors with internal solder lugs rather than simple twist-and-tape repairs.

If the wiring inspection reveals no obvious faults but the issue persists, consider the possibility of ground loop interference. The remote starter adds new grounds; if these are connected to a different chassis point than the factory ECU or body control module grounds, potential differences can cause erratic behavior in shared power domains. Ensure all new grounds are bonded directly to clean, unpainted metal on the chassis with thick gauge wire.

Before removing the system entirely, verify that the factory fuse for the ignition accessory circuit hasn't blown due to a shorted accessory in the remote starter harness. Check the fuse box for any fuses labeled "ACC," "IGN," or specific cluster feeds. If the remote starter was not grounded correctly, it could have back-fed voltage into sensitive lines, causing a fuse to blow intermittently as heat degraded the internal element.

If you determine that the installation quality is beyond repair or if multiple splice points are failing, uninstalling the RS90 and returning to factory operation might be the only reliable path forward. The trade-off here is losing the convenience of remote start for winter mornings, but regaining 100% electrical reliability in a vehicle that is two decades old. A poorly integrated aftermarket accessory can destabilize an aging electrical architecture faster than it enhances functionality.
